newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU offers blueprint for capital markets under EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU offers blueprint for capital markets under EMU.

text.p: The European Commission put forward on Wednesday a possible blueprint for how European bond and share markets might operate after a single currency is introduced on January 1, 1999.

Compiling the input from months of discussions among financial market experts, the Commission's report offered a series of recommendations on the technical aspects -- such as redenomination of government debt -- of European capital markets after monetary union.

Specifically, the group of experts chaired by Alberto Giovannini of Long-Term Capital Management Group in London, said the redenomination of government debt should take place via a "bottom-up" approach -- directly converting the overall value of bond holdings from national currencies into the euro.

Germany on Tuesday said it was likely to redenominate its outstanding debt beginning on the start date in 1999. Only France, Belgium and Luxembourg have said they would convert old debt, but the broad expectation is that most others will follow.
Herve Carre, monetary affairs director at the Commission, said the bottom-up approach would minimise the risk associated with rounding calculations.
Regarding bond markets, the report also offered the following conclusions:

-- The method used for calculating interest on bonds should be based on the actual number of days in the months over which the interest has accrued divided by the actual number of days in the year -- otherwise known as "actual/actual."

-- Business days should be harmonised among countries participating in the euro. The option favoured would be the operating days proposed for the clearing system of the future European Central Bank. In practice this would probably mean that markets will function for all but two business holidays -- Christmas and New Year's Day.
-- Markets will need to decide, "on the basis of quality, liquidity and the range of products available," which country should be the benchmark issuer for euro-denominated debt.

-- The need for harmonisation of coupon payments and settlement periods was not seen as essential. "Maintaining existing national practices would not create difficulties for the operation of markets in the euro zone," the report said.
For equity markets, there was the expectation that European exchanges will trade and quote in the euro from day one.

But coordination and harmonisation of market rules and conventions was not seen to be as urgent as for bond markets, with the timing of the redenomination of share values a decision for each individual company.

Commission officials did not see the need for EU regulations to implement such market rules. Instead, it would be up to financial markets to decide on the most effective means for issuing and trading debt and shares in the euro area.
Meanwhile, governments not participating in the euro would also be free to issue or redenominate debt from their national currencies into the single currency.
